legal_full:
Preamble. We are building an open map where people around the globe share dosimeter readings for the common good — science, ecology, education, and safety. By publishing your data you help many. Please treat this shared work with care.

1) Responsibility. The accuracy and content of any information you submit remain your responsibility. Data are published and used “as is”. The service does not confirm or guarantee their correctness, completeness, or suitability for any purpose and bears no responsibility for any possible outcome of their use.

2) Openness and license. By sharing dosimetry readings, dates, approximate locations, device models, or other facts, you understand they become available to everyone and may be used freely under the CC0 1.0 (Public Domain) license for data, while the code remains available under the MIT license. Authorship stays with you; no compensation is provided; further redistribution by third parties is beyond our control.

3) “As is” and no verification. Publications appear without prior review. We cannot guarantee instrument calibration or the absence of mistakes. The information is shared for research and is not a professional recommendation.

4) Privacy and moderation. To keep the map safe and trustworthy, timestamps and coordinates may be generalized, and technical metadata may be removed or anonymized. We may hide or delete materials that, in our reasonable opinion, are spam, falsified, unlawful, or disruptive. We handle bona fide measurements with care and strive to preserve them.

5) Cookies. The site relies on a short-lived technical session cookie; it disappears when your visit ends. We do not keep any other traces.

Friends, this map is the result of shared effort and open hearts. Please treat it as a sketch of the terrain, not a precise blueprint. If our work resonates with you, join in — together we can make it better.
legend_full:
📍 How to read the radiation map

The map's colour scale deliberately makes background radiation visible and understandable, so everyone can assess conditions at a particular location and make their own decisions about living there, visiting and radiation risks.

The map does not divide radiation into “safe natural” and “dangerous artificial” radiation: at the same dose, natural radiation can also pose a risk. Causes may include geology, radon and natural radionuclides, or artificial contamination, industry, nuclear power and accidents.

A green zone does not guarantee the complete absence of risk and reflects only the measurements currently available. The colour helps you make an informed decision: spend less time there, limit local water and food, take protective measures or decide against living in the area long term if the risk seems unacceptable.

The map aims both to show existing contamination and to help society avoid creating new contamination and treat the environment more carefully.

🟩
0–11

Green zone

“Generally normal external gamma background”

0–11 microroentgens per hour is typical of many places with an ordinary natural gamma background.

  • Residence: external gamma background alone generally imposes no special restrictions on permanent residence.
  • Water: a normal local gamma background is not itself a reason to avoid local water, but boreholes and springs should ideally be tested at least once for chemical composition, uranium and, where the geology warrants it, radon.
  • Gardening and local food: local produce can generally be grown and eaten if there are no known contamination sources.
  • Mushrooms and berries: in areas with historical radioactive fallout, forest mushrooms and some berries can accumulate more caesium-137 than ordinary agricultural crops.
  • Home: even on a green map, measuring indoor radon is advisable, especially on the ground floor, in basements and in houses built directly on the ground.
  • Tritium: an ordinary gamma dosimeter detects almost none of it. Tritium monitoring is especially relevant where water is hydrologically connected to a nuclear facility or a known discharge or leak site.
🟨
11–30

Yellow zone

“Be alert and understand the cause”

11–30 microroentgens per hour corresponds to up to roughly 2.7 mSv/year, or 2.7 times the annual additional public dose limit of 1000 microsieverts per year, with continuous exposure to such an external radiation field.

  • Residence: this level usually does not indicate immediate danger, but before living there for many years it is advisable to understand why the area differs from average background levels.
  • Water: if you use your own borehole, well or spring, laboratory testing is sensible, especially in uranium-bearing, granitic and radon-prone areas.
  • Food: when a local increase persists, know where local vegetables, milk, meat and other foods come from.
  • Mushrooms and berries: in areas affected by old radioactive fallout, test them separately; forest ecosystems can retain radiocaesium for decades.
  • Radon: measure it inside the home rather than trying to detect it with an ordinary dosimeter.
  • Tritium: near nuclear facilities or downstream of them, separate laboratory water monitoring is useful where there are grounds for concern.
🟥
30–100

Red zone

“Investigate before making it your permanent home”

30–100 microroentgens per hour corresponds to roughly 2.7–9.1 mSv/year, or 2.7–9.1 times the annual additional public dose limit of 1000 microsieverts per year, if exposure is genuinely continuous.

  • Residence: long-term permanent residence is inadvisable without identifying the source of the elevated background.
  • Water: do not regularly drink local groundwater or surface water merely because it is clear and tastes good. Testing is needed if contamination is suspected.
  • Gardening: before growing food continuously on one plot, test the soil and understand which radionuclides are causing the anomaly.
  • Local food: confirmed contamination calls for monitoring vegetables, milk, meat and other staple foods.
  • Mushrooms and berries: regular harvesting in contaminated areas is particularly inadvisable without testing; some mushroom species accumulate radiocaesium efficiently.
  • Tobacco: growing and smoking local tobacco from contaminated soil is an especially poor idea. Tobacco leaves may contain radioactive polonium-210 and lead-210, which enter the lungs directly when smoked.
  • Radon: if the high background is associated with uranium-bearing rocks, test indoor air and groundwater.
⬛
100+

Black zone

“Do not stay long without understanding the source”

More than 100 microroentgens per hour indicates a pronounced increase in external gamma background. 110 microroentgens per hour ≈ 10 mSv/year (10 times the annual additional public dose limit of 1000 microsieverts per year, or half the average annual occupational exposure limit over a five-year period) with continuous exposure.

  • Residence: reduce time spent there and identify the source before deciding to live there permanently.
  • Water and food: do not regularly use local food and water without understanding the nature of the contamination.
  • Gardening, mushrooms and berries: appearance alone does not establish safety; contamination requires radiological testing.
  • Dust: avoid inhaling it or bringing it home, because internal contamination may matter more than the external dose rate.
  • Important: 100 microroentgens per hour is not a level that causes immediate radiation injury. The main concern is unnecessary long-term exposure and possible environmental contamination.

The essentials from the outset

  • The map's number does not show the entire radiation hazard, only the radiation that the particular instrument can detect.
  • Risk depends on dose rate, exposure duration, radiation type and how radioactive substances enter the body.
  • Even a completely green map may miss factors that an ordinary gamma dosimeter barely detects: radon, tritium, alpha emitters, neutrons, some beta emitters and dissolved radionuclides in water.
  • Beyond a short-term dose, long-term residence matters especially: what a person breathes daily, which water they drink and which local foods they eat over the years.
  • The map is a guide and a tool for finding anomalies, not a universal guarantee of safety.

📐 Quick conversion for constant gamma background

Simplified formula: mSv/year ≈ µR/h ÷ 11.

  • 11 µR/h ≈ 1 mSv/year
  • 30 µR/h ≈ 2.7 mSv/year — about 2.7 times the annual limit for additional regulated public dose
  • 60 µR/h ≈ 5.5 mSv/year — about 5.5 such annual limits
  • 110 µR/h ≈ 10 mSv/year — about 10 such annual limits
  • 220 µR/h ≈ 20 mSv/year — equal to the average annual occupational exposure limit over a five-year period

Important: this is only an approximate conversion for a constant external photon field, mainly gamma radiation, experienced 24 hours a day throughout the year. Natural background and medical exposure are counted separately. Do not apply it to neutrons, protons or a complex cosmic radiation field.

⚖️ Regulatory reference levels

  • Public exposure: 1000 microsieverts per year of additional regulated effective dose
  • Occupationally exposed workers: an average of 20 000 microsieverts per year over five years
  • For workers in any single year: no more than 50 000 microsieverts

These are radiation protection limits, not a sharp biological boundary between “safe” and “dangerous”. The less unnecessary additional dose, the better.

🏠 Radon: the main invisible problem in many homes

Radon is a colourless, odourless radioactive gas produced as uranium decays in soil and rock. It quickly disperses outdoors but can accumulate in an enclosed house.

Radon often enters through foundation cracks, joints, service entry points, basements and other places where the building contacts the ground.

  • Ventilation usually helps lower indoor radon concentrations, although high levels may require a dedicated system.
  • A basement is not automatically dangerous, but lower rooms should be measured first.
  • New buildings in radon-prone areas benefit from a sealed slab or membrane, sealed service entry points and a system that vents soil gas from beneath the building outdoors (construction on ventilated piles).
  • A house with a well-ventilated crawl space or minimal contact between living areas and the ground may reduce soil-gas entry, but piles alone offer no guarantee; radon must still be measured after construction.

The simplest rule: an ordinary gamma-background map cannot reveal radon; measure it indoors with a dedicated radon detector.

🚰 Radon and natural radionuclides in groundwater

Boreholes, wells and springs pass through large volumes of rock. Groundwater can therefore contain radon, uranium, radium and other natural radionuclides.

Radon is generally more common and more concentrated in groundwater than in surface water. When this water is used, some radon escapes into the air, especially during showers, heating and vigorous mixing.

For radon in water, ingestion is not the only route; subsequent inhalation of radon released from water into indoor air is often more significant.

An ordinary gamma dosimeter beside a bottle of water may show nothing unusual. A reliable assessment requires laboratory analysis.

🌱 Gardening, plants and transfer of radionuclides from soil to food

Radioactive soil contamination does not stay only in the ground. Some radionuclides can enter plants through their roots and then pass to animals and people.

The extent of transfer depends on the particular radionuclide and plant, soil acidity and composition, potassium and calcium content, organic matter and other factors.

  • Caesium behaves somewhat like potassium chemically and can enter biological processes.
  • Strontium and radium are chemically similar to calcium and can pass into plants and subsequently into animal and human bone tissue.
  • Different crops may differ greatly in their ability to accumulate the same radionuclide.

With confirmed contamination of agricultural land, test the soil itself and the harvested food rather than drawing conclusions solely from the gamma dose rate above the plot.

🍄 Mushrooms and berries are a separate matter

Forest foods can behave differently from garden produce. Some mushroom species readily accumulate caesium-137, and elevated activity can persist for decades after radioactive fallout.

Accumulation depends strongly on the mushroom species and location. Neither assume all mushrooms are equally contaminated nor judge their safety solely from a dosimeter reading on a nearby path.

Wild berries can also transfer radionuclides from forest soil. In known fallout areas, consult local laboratory monitoring results.

🚬 Tobacco and radioactive substances

Tobacco and other nightshade plants are particularly undesirable routes for internal intake of radioactive substances. Their leaves can accumulate radionuclides especially strongly, including polonium-210 and lead-210.

Smoking carries some of these substances directly into the respiratory tract with the smoke. Growing tobacco and other nightshade plants on land suspected of radioactive contamination and then smoking the tobacco is therefore a poor practice.

This adds a radiation-related factor to the already well-known chemical risks of tobacco smoke.

☢️ External and internal exposure are fundamentally different

External exposure is relatively easy to stop: if the distant source remains in the area, leave the elevated-dose-rate zone, increase your distance or use shielding.

If radioactive dust remains on clothing or skin, however, that is contamination, and the source effectively travels with the person.

Internal exposure is more complicated. Radioactive substances can reach the lungs in dust and aerosols, the digestive tract in water and food, or enter through damaged skin.

Unstable nuclei then continue decaying directly inside the body until the substance is excreted or decays.

🧬 What radiation does inside a cell

Alpha and beta particles cause ionisation: they knock electrons out of molecules and initiate chemical reactions.

  • DNA stores genetic information. Radiation can alter its molecules and break its strands.
  • The cell membrane regulates exchange between the cell and its surroundings and can also be damaged.
  • Organelles are internal cell structures, such as mitochondria, which produce energy.
  • Free radicals, including those produced by water radiolysis, can damage DNA, proteins and membranes.

Alpha emitters inside the body are especially important: an alpha particle scarcely penetrates skin from outside, but deposits substantial energy over a very short distance within tissue.

💧 Tritium: radioactive hydrogen in water

Tritium, ³H, is a radioactive hydrogen isotope with a half-life of about 12.3 years. It emits very low-energy beta radiation.

Small amounts of tritium form naturally in the atmosphere continuously under cosmic radiation. Significant artificial quantities can form in nuclear reactors and other nuclear installations.

Depending on reactor type, tritium forms in fuel, coolant and other materials. It can enter process water and then appear in permitted controlled discharges or leaks.

Tritiated water, HTO, is particularly important environmentally. Chemically it is almost indistinguishable from ordinary water and joins the normal water cycle: evaporation, atmospheric transport, precipitation and entry into rivers, soil, plants and living organisms.

That is why ordinary household filters cannot simply “filter out” tritium from water as though it were a solid impurity.

🧬 Tritium inside the body

Once ingested, tritiated water distributes with ordinary body water and can reach virtually all soft tissues.

Most is excreted relatively quickly, but some tritium can become incorporated into organic molecules and remain longer.

Tritium beta particles penetrate very poorly from outside. Decay directly inside a cell, however, releases energy beside biological molecules and can cause ionisation and DNA damage.

Germ cells, the cell lineage that produces sperm and eggs, are especially relevant. DNA damage in such a cell could theoretically persist in hereditary material.

🔬 Why tritium is hard to detect

Tritium's beta radiation is so weak that an ordinary gamma dosimeter will hardly detect tritium in water.

One standard method is liquid scintillation spectrometry:

  1. Prepare and purify the water sample.
  2. Mix it with a special scintillation solution.
  3. Beta decays produce extremely faint flashes of light.
  4. A low-background instrument counts these flashes under carefully controlled conditions.

Very low concentrations may require lengthy measurements and prior tritium concentration.

🧊 Old ice and tritium decay

If water is isolated from new tritium inputs, its activity continuously declines:

  • After 12.3 years, about 50% remains.
  • After 25 years, about 25% remains.
  • After 100 years, less than 1% remains.
  • After several hundred years, the original tritium has practically disappeared.

Ancient ice may therefore contain extremely little of the tritium present in the water when it formed.

But the absence of tritium does not automatically make water drinkable: microbiological, chemical and other radiological criteria still apply.

⛏️ Uranium and in-situ leaching

In uranium mining by ISR/ISL — in-situ recovery or leaching, a solution is injected into the ore-bearing layer to make uranium water-soluble, then pumped back out.

This deliberately increases uranium mobility in groundwater and may alter the mobility of other elements.

In areas of current or historical uranium mining, groundwater monitoring is therefore especially important; a low external gamma background alone does not make a well safe.

☄️ Cosmic protons and neutrons

Primary cosmic radiation consists mainly of energetic protons and atomic nuclei. Collisions with the atmosphere produce secondary neutrons, protons, muons, electrons and gamma photons.

At altitudes of roughly 9–12 km, the effective dose rate is often about 4–8 microsieverts per hour (400–800 microroentgens per hour). Under some conditions, neutrons account for a substantial part of this dose.

For example, 5 microsieverts per hour × 700 flight hours = about 3500 microsieverts per year, or roughly 3.5 times the annual additional public dose limit of 1000 microsieverts per year.

For flight crews, this exposure is occupationally significant and is accounted for through accumulated dose.

📡 Why ordinary dosimeters measure neutrons poorly

Neutrons have no electric charge, so an ordinary gamma counter is poorly suited to detecting them.

Fast neutrons require a hydrogen-rich moderator, such as polyethylene or water, followed by a dedicated neutron-sensitive element based, for example, on boron-10, lithium-6 or helium-3.

Polyethylene alone around a household gamma dosimeter is insufficient for a complete neutron-dose measurement.

⚛️ Neutron activation

A neutron can interact directly with an atomic nucleus. Some reactions turn a stable isotope into a radioactive one; this is called neutron activation.

This is especially important in nuclear reactors, where neutron flux is very high and structural materials can indeed become radioactive.

At aviation altitudes, induced radioactivity in the human body is negligible; the principal factor is the dose received directly from the cosmic radiation field.

🌍 Why cosmic radiation is lower at Earth's surface

  • Earth's magnetic field deflects some charged cosmic particles.
  • The magnetic field does not directly deflect neutrons.
  • The atmosphere provides a vast thickness of material in which cosmic particles interact and lose energy.
  • Soil, water, concrete and rock provide additional shielding against external radiation.

Geomagnetic protection is weaker near the poles, so the cosmic dose at the same altitude is usually higher.

⏳ Time is the main multiplier of dose

Dose rate shows how quickly a person receives dose. 110 microroentgens per hour ≈ 10 mSv/year only with continuous exposure at that level throughout the year.

Internal contamination is more complicated: radioactive material is already inside the body and may keep irradiating tissues for days, months or years.

🗺️ Why the map cannot be trusted blindly

Even a perfectly green map reflects only the part of the radiation situation measured by the instrument.

It does not replace radon measurement, tritium analysis, neutron dosimetry or testing of water, soil, mushrooms, berries and other foods where these are warranted.

👉 For long-term residence, consider both the external background number and the entire exposure pathway: home → air → water → soil → plants → local food → body.
legend_safecast_description: This is the traditional radiation level color scale adopted by safecast.org in 2013 and used consistently on their maps since then. Users of safecast.org find it intuitive. The wide color range allows subtle differences to be distinguished instantly at a glance, and the logarithmic scale helps users easily see relatively small differences in radiation levels near natural background while also displaying levels several orders of magnitude higher.

Add your measurement track to the map. We support .kml, .kmz, .gpx, .csv, .rctrk, .json, .log, as well as RadiaCode, AtomFast, and SafeCast dosimeters.
